content: I'm bundling Std.Internal.List.DistinctKeys with an association list and I'm using the structure of the Std.DHashMap codebase as a blueprint, so as to eventually have a non-dependent and a set version. I've noticed: most of the theorems of Std.DHashMap.contains don't use the Membership.mem notation, yet the left-to-right simp annotation on Std.DHashMap.contains_iff_mem suggests that expressions involving Std.DHashMap.contains are to be simplified towards Membership.mem. Why then are most of the theorems of Std.DHashMap.contains written with itself instead of being formulated in terms of Membership.mem? Would it be bad practice to emulate e.g. List.contains and to minimize theorems that mention contains?
contains is a Bool, while Mem is a Prop. They are not the same thing. docs#Std.DHashMap.contains_iff_mem says that if you "cast" contains from a bool to a prop, then you get Mem.

By the way, as the name suggests, docs#Std.Internal.List.DistinctKeys is an internal type, not a stable base to build your library on. It will keep changing with no warnings or deprecations. We might even remove it.

Thank you for the answer! right, *.contains is a Bool and Membership.mem is a Prop, but while for List.contains the relationship between the two requires a LawfulBEq instance, the Membership.mem instance for the hash types doesn't need any law-abiding instances, so it seems to me they are isomorphic for all intents and purposes (e.g. Std.DHashMap.contains returns Bool.true iff the membership proposition is satisfied)

and ty for the comment wrt Std.Internal.List.DistinctKeys. although the instability might be inconvenient, there is atm no other extensive theory of simple association lists so I'll be assuming the responsibility of checking for changes

Yes, they have the same information, but there is an issue of ergonomics here. Freely mixing Bool and Prop terms works for a while because the elaborator will insert = true and decide as appropriate, but at some point the simplifier can get confused and things don't cancel/lemmas don't apply. So the hash map library gives you the opportunity to be mindful about which to use when and get simp lemmas that match the variant you choose
hm that makes sense, I'll be delving deeper to see how the two simpsets interact. thanks for the answers!
